# Latitude from Pole Star and noon Sun (quadrant, astrolabe, cross-staff, kamal) (`latitude_astrolabe_quadrant`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by world_geography, map_projection_charts, trigonometry
- Core idea: Latitude is the signed altitude of the celestial pole. North of the equator, measure Polaris with a quadrant and plumb line. In 1490 the star circles roughly 3.5° from the pole, so pilots use the orientation of nearby stars to correct the reading. At local apparent noon measure the Sun's altitude by its shadow and take its solar declination for the date (north positive). The zenith distance is 90° minus the altitude. If the Sun culminates south of the observer, add the zenith distance to the declination. If it culminates north, subtract it. At the zenith latitude equals declination. A quadrant measures altitude against a plumb line. On a mariner’s astrolabe, the sighting rule turns against a graduated vertical disc. A one-degree error means about 60 nautical miles north or south. Portuguese navigators had tried solar observations in Guinea by 1485. Zacuto's astronomical tables existed in manuscript by 1478, and the printed Almanach perpetuum followed in 1496. A suspended instrument works better ashore than on a pitching deck. Reaching a known latitude and following it east or west can guide a landfall without giving longitude.
- Pitfalls:
  - Forgetting the Sun's declination, which swings between +23.4° and −23.4° over the year; without the table the noon method is useless
  - Taking the Pole Star as exactly at the pole in 1490 (3.5° off then, about 0.7° today)
  - Expecting minute accuracy from a rolling deck; at sea 1° was good with quadrant or astrolabe, and the plumb line swings (Columbus's readings in Cuba were wildly wrong)
  - Using the Pole Star south of the equator; it is invisible there, the noon Sun and suitable southern stars give alternatives
  - Looking straight into the Sun with a cross-staff; use the backstaff (Davis 1594) or the astrolabe's shadow pinholes
- History: islamic: c. 1490 – Ibn Majid gives star altitudes in finger units (isba, about 1.6°) measured with the kamal, a wooden board on a knotted cord; china: early 15th c. – Zheng He's charts give star altitudes in 'fingers' measured with star-boards (qianxing ban); europe: c. 1460 – Portuguese pilots measure the Pole Star with the quadrant; 1485 José Vizinho measures noon Sun latitudes in Guinea; 1496 Zacuto's Almanach perpetuum; mariner's astrolabes in Portuguese navigation by the late 1480s (Sodré astrolabe dated c. 1496–1501, recovered from a 1503 wreck); c. 1509 printed Regimento do astrolábio; cross-staff at sea from c. 1514; global: Pacific – Polynesian navigators use zenith stars passing overhead to know the latitude of an island
- Read:
  - David L. Mearns, Jason M. Warnett and Mark A. Williams, An Early Portuguese Mariner's Astrolabe from the Sodré Wreck-site, Al Hallaniyah, Oman (2019)
  - Abraham Zacuto, Almanach perpetuum (1496)
  - David W. Waters, The Art of Navigation in England in Elizabethan and Early Stuart Times (1958)
  - G. R. Tibbetts, Arab Navigation in the Indian Ocean before the Coming of the Portuguese (1971)
